title: Do Pathology Foundation Models Encode Disease Progression? A Pseudotime Analysis of Visual Representations
claim: Embedding static samples with a foundation model and applying pseudotime recovers ordinal progression, quantified by a single rank-correlation fidelity score.
layout: 3 stages left-to-right: input patches, model box, analysis panel with paired scatters and score
description: A left-to-right evaluation pipeline. On the far left, five H&E pathology patches are framed in colored borders and labeled Epidermis, AK, SCC, Epidermis and CIS. Gray arrows lead to a rounded box labeled Foundation Model, which has stacked blue bars as its icon. A large blue-outlined panel titled Diffusion Pseudotime Analysis follows. It holds two side-by-side scatter plots on DC1 and DC2 axes. The first is colored by discrete class (red, blue, green, purple). The second is colored by continuous pseudotime on a blue-to-red gradient. Both show a V-shaped manifold with a connecting trajectory line through class centroids. At the right, a large blue 'τ = 0.72' sits above the label Trajectory Fidelity and an italic explanation of the score's range, from 1 for perfect ordering to -1 for reversed.
caption: Overview of trajectory fidelity evaluation. H&E patches representing disease states (here: skin squamous cell carcinoma progression from epidermis through actinic keratosis and carcinoma in situ to invasive SCC) are embedded by a foundation model (Virchow-2). We apply diffusion pseudotime analysis to the embedding space, visualized here via diffusion components (DC1, DC2). Left: patches colored by ground-truth class; Right: the same embeddings colored by inferred pseudotime. Trajectory fidelity (τ, Kendall’s rank correlation) quantifies agreement between pseudotime ordering and ground-truth ordinal class labels.
abstract: Vision foundation models trained on discretely sampled images achieve strong performance on classification benchmarks, yet whether their representations encode the continuous processes underlying their training data remains unclear. This question is especially pertinent in computational pathology, where we posit that models whose latent representations implicitly capture ordinal disease progression may better reflect underlying biology, support more robust generalization, and enable quantitative analyses of features associated with disease transitions. Using diffusion pseudotime, a method developed to infer developmental trajectories from single-cell transcriptomics, we probe whether foundation models organize disease states along coherent progression directions in representation space. Across four cancer progressions and six models, we find that all pathology-specific models recover trajectory orderings significantly exceeding null baselines, with pathology vision-only models achieving the highest average fidelities. Model rankings by trajectory fidelity on reference diseases predict few-shot classification performance on held-out diseases ($Ï= 0.91$), and exploratory analysis shows cell-type composition varies along inferred trajectories in patterns consistent with known stromal remodeling. Together, these results suggest that vision foundation models can implicitly learn to represent continuous processes from independent static observations, and that trajectory fidelity provides a complementary measure of representation quality beyond downstream performance. While demonstrated in pathology, this framework could be applied to other domains where continuous processes are observed through static snapshots.
